documents.title: AI in the Syllabus
tiers: Example 1: AI used with co-created class agreement and citation format
Example 2: AI encouraged, with required AI Acknowledgement
Example 3: AI not used unless directed (foundational skills)

documents.summary: Teaching-center guidance that explains why blanket AI bans are hard to enforce and may hinder skills, then offers four sample syllabus statements from open use to restriction. It leaves the stance to each instructor and recommends discussing it on day one.
documents.stance_why: The page sets no single rule: it says 'AI syllabus policies should be being clear, flexible, learner-centered and process-focused' and offers four sample statements ranging from 'encourages and embraces' to 'not to be used ... unless specifically directed', so the decision is left to instructors.

units.why: The overview says students 'stand a good chance of encountering different AI policies' across courses, a fact that AI rules vary by course; I chose P11 (course rules are course-specific) because the point is variation between courses.
units.anchor: students who take more than one course in a semester stand a good chance of
units.fit_note: States as a fact that policies differ across courses; does not itself say one course's rules do not carry over. Describes that policies differ across courses rather than stating that one course's rule does not carry over.

units.why: The overview says that 'by producing a clear AI statement and discussing it with students on the first day of class', instructors can ensure students have the information they need. This recommends both writing and discussing the rule with students; the discussion is the distinctive part, so P66 rather than P09 (which requires a statement in every syllabus, something this page does not do).
units.anchor: producing a clear AI statement and discussing it with students on the first day of
units.policy: Instructors produce a clear AI statement and discuss it with students on the first day of class or in the introductory module of an asynchronous course.
units.fit_note: Also recommends producing a clear written AI statement (P09); the page does not make the statement mandatory.
units.resolution_why: A coded P66 (explain and discuss), B coded P09 (statement in syllabus). The source recommends a clear statement and discussing it on day one; it does not require a statement (that is the MOA), so P66 fits and the written-statement part goes in fit_note. unit_stance set to neutral because the passage takes no position on AI use itself (A said encourage).

units.why: The page warns that 'it may be tempting to take a prohibitive classroom policy stance' but that this 'is problematic (and potentially unethical)'; this advises against blanket bans, which no listed type captures (P03 discourages AI, the opposite direction).
units.anchor: it may be tempting to take a prohibitive classroom policy stance against the use of
units.frag_start: To that end, it may be tempting
units.policy: Taking a prohibitive classroom policy stance against the use of AI tools is problematic (and potentially unethical).
units.fit_note: Advises instructors against prohibiting AI; it does not state an allow-by-default rule for students.
units.uncovered_note: Advises instructors against adopting a blanket prohibitive AI policy because it is problematic and potentially unethical.
units.resolution_why: A coded UNCOVERED, B coded P02; both gave actor instructor, phase before-course, should-not, permit. The source says it 'may be tempting to take a prohibitive classroom policy stance' but 'that is problematic (and potentially unethical)'. That is advice against banning AI, not a default-allow rule (B's own fit note says so), and no existing type states it, so UNCOVERED with a note follows; a normalized policy is added because the anchor stops before the conclusion.

units.why: The page says detection is "nearly impossible" so AI use cannot be enforced "with any consistency or validity"; this states a limit on control, which P82 covers, rather than a detector rule (P39), which the next unit codes.
units.anchor: it is nearly impossible to detect, and therefore enforce, the use of AI with any
units.resolution_why: Same type P82 and phase in both. A coded actor all, B coded instructor. The page is guidance addressed to instructors choosing a policy, so instructor is kept. Topics merged from both.

units.why: "Rigorous testing has shown that AI detectors are unreliable in most practical scenarios" says detectors cannot be trusted as proof; this is P39 (do not rely on detectors) stated as a fact, so modality informs.
units.anchor: AI detectors are unreliable in most practical scenarios
units.resolution_why: Same type P39; A coded actor all, B instructor. The sentence is evidence offered to instructors deciding how to enforce, so instructor.

units.why: The page says 'AI detectors have also been shown to be biased against English language learners', a further reason not to rely on detectors, aimed at instructors choosing how to enforce. It is a fact (informs) about detectors, so P39 (do not rely on detectors) with an equity topic.
units.anchor: AI detectors have also been shown to be biased against English language learners
units.frag_start: AI detectors have also been shown
units.fit_note: Adds a specific bias against English language learners as a reason detectors are unreliable. The bias is in detectors, not in generative AI itself.
units.resolution_why: A coded P39, B coded P53 (bias, harms). The bias named is in the detectors, not in generative AI (B's fit note), and the sentence supports not relying on detectors, so P39 fits better; the bias detail goes in fit_note. Actor set to instructor as in unit 4 (A said all).

units.why: The page warns that 'the restrictions you impose may hinder the development of skills and behaviors needed to engage thoughtfully in an AI-integrated world'. It is a reason, addressed to instructors who are deciding what to impose, so it is rationale (informs) under P44 (effective AI use as a skill).
units.anchor: hinder the development of skills and behaviors needed to engage thoughtfully in an AI-integrated world
units.fit_note: Framed as a cost of banning AI, not as a statement that courses should teach AI use.
units.resolution_why: Same actor and type. A coded phase before-course, B general. The sentence speaks to instructors deciding what restrictions to impose, which is policy design, so before-course. B's anchor kept as the fuller span.

units.why: The page says 'one approach educators are using' is 'to require students who use AI to reflect on and cite their use of AI tools'. This offers requiring disclosure as an option to instructors who do not prohibit AI, so it is P24 with modality may.

units.fit_note: Also includes reflection and sharing process and prompts (P26, P25); presented as one approach educators use, not as a rule. Also mentions reflection and citing prompts (P25, P26).

The passage presents the practice as an option instructors can adopt in place of banning ('Rather than all out prohibiting AI usage'), not a rule and not mere fact, so may. The anchor states the practice, so policy is null.

documents.title: MOA 2514 revision: syllabus AI requirements
documents.summary: A Faculty Senate memorandum, signed March 2026, that adds a required AI statement to the list of syllabus elements. It requires instructors to state their AI expectations explicitly and treats unauthorized or undisclosed AI use as an academic integrity violation under the Student Code.
documents.stance_why: The memorandum says it will 'require faculty to explicitly state how AI can and cannot be used in the classroom without dictating what that looks like for faculty', so it sets no stance and hands the decision to instructors.
